title: Challenge 07: Survive a Merge Conflict
description: Reading conflict markers, choosing content, deleting markers, and committing a resolution.
concepts: Reading conflict markers, choosing content, deleting markers, and committing a resolution.
Challenge title: Survive a Merge Conflict
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're doing something that sounds dramatic but is actually very ordinary in Git and GitHub: surviving a merge conflict.

[JAMIE]
I appreciate that wording, because "merge conflict" sounds like I broke the internet.

[ALEX]
Exactly. But a merge conflict is not a failure. It's a checkpoint. Git is simply saying, "Two changes overlap, and I need a human decision."

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Here's the big picture. In this lesson, we'll cover what a merge conflict is, why it happens, how to prevent it, how to read the conflict markers, how to resolve conflicts on GitHub, how VS Code helps, what to do in the terminal if you work locally, and what to do when you feel stuck.

[JAMIE]
And for this course specifically, there's a controlled practice challenge, right?

[ALEX]
Right. This chapter uses one short practice challenge so you can learn conflict resolution in a low-pressure way. The pattern is: observe, resolve, verify. The time expectation is under ten minutes. Your evidence is an issue-linked pull request and a completion comment.

[JAMIE]
So the goal isn't just "make the warning go away." It's to understand the structure, make a decision, and prove you resolved it cleanly.

[ALEX]
That's it.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
For the challenge, your facilitator triggers a merge conflict in your pull request. You open the PR, look for the conflict notice, choose Resolve conflicts or edit the file directly on your branch, find the conflict markers, decide what content belongs in the final file, delete the marker lines, and commit the resolution.

[JAMIE]
And the autograder is looking for two things: no conflict markers left behind, and meaningful content still in the file.

[ALEX]
Yes. So if you remove everything, that's not success. And if you leave even one marker line, that's not success either.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's define the core idea. A merge conflict happens when two people change the same part of the same file in different ways, and Git cannot automatically decide which version to keep.

[JAMIE]
So if I edit line twelve and you edit line two hundred, Git usually handles that fine.

[ALEX]
Usually, yes. But if we both edit the same line, or nearby lines in a way that overlaps, Git may stop and ask for help.

[JAMIE]
What are the common reasons this happens?

[ALEX]
A few classics: two people edited the same line, one person deleted a file while another edited it, two people restructured the same section, or a branch stayed open too long and drifted far away from main.

[JAMIE]
That last one feels especially realistic in open source.

[ALEX]
Very realistic. Long-running branches invite conflicts.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Before we resolve conflicts, let's make them less likely. Prevention is easier than resolution.

[JAMIE]
Give us the practical list.

[ALEX]
Keep branches short-lived. Aim for small, focused work that merges in a few days, not a few weeks.

Sync with main frequently. From your feature branch, you may merge origin slash main into your branch. And if you're comfortable with rebasing, rebasing onto origin slash main is another option.

Communicate with your team. If you know you'll be editing a heavily used file, say so.

Avoid mass reformatting unless it's coordinated, because changing lots of lines creates unnecessary overlap.

Pull before you push, so you're not building on stale history.

Work on separate files when possible.

Keep pull requests small.

And use draft pull requests for early visibility, so other contributors can see what area you're touching before things collide.

[JAMIE]
That's a strong pattern: short branches, frequent sync, small PRs, visible work.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Those habits reduce stress.

[JAMIE]
And there was also an advanced prevention idea about fast-forward merges.

[ALEX]
Yes. The important concept is that simpler branch histories can reduce complexity. You don't need to master fast-forward behavior today, but it helps to know that the shape of history affects how cleanly changes integrate.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Okay. Now let's talk about the thing learners actually see: conflict markers.

[ALEX]
Yes. When Git can't merge automatically, it inserts plain-text markers directly into the file.

Here is the classic shape:

Less-than signs repeated seven times, then HEAD.
Then one version of the content.
Then a separator line made of equals signs.
Then the other version of the content.
Then greater-than signs repeated seven times, followed by a branch name.

[JAMIE]
And because this is an audio lesson, let's label the sections clearly.

[ALEX]
Good idea. There are three important parts.

First, the section between the start marker and the separator.

Second, the section between the separator and the end marker.

Third, the marker lines themselves.

In the solution reference, the section between the start marker and the separator is described as the version on the branch you are merging into, usually main. The section between the separator and the end marker is the version on your branch.

[JAMIE]
But in the practice chapter instructions, the wording says the first block is your version, the current branch, and the second block is their version, the incoming branch.

[ALEX]
Right, and that's why context matters. Different tools and workflows describe the sides a little differently depending on where the merge is happening. The safe habit is this: do not rely only on labels like "yours" and "theirs." Read the actual text on both sides and decide what final content should remain.

[JAMIE]
That's helpful, especially for learners who worry about memorizing the wrong mapping.

[ALEX]
Exactly. The universally safe truth is: the marker lines are not content, and the final file must contain only the text you actually want to keep.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's make that concrete with the example resolution from the reference solution.

Suppose one side says, "Welcome to the Learning Room. This is the main branch version."
The other side says, "Welcome to the Learning Room. This is my improved version with more detail."

Your options are threefold.

Keep yours: delete the other section and all marker lines.

Keep theirs: delete your section and all marker lines.

Or combine both: write one clean final version that incorporates the best parts of each.

[JAMIE]
So there is not always one magic correct answer.

[ALEX]
Correct. The decision depends on what is better for the project. Two valid resolutions may use different wording.

[JAMIE]
That fits the peer simulation note too. It's okay if your final wording differs from someone else's, as long as it's a valid resolution.

[ALEX]
Exactly right.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now let's walk through the challenge flow step by step.

First, wait for your facilitator to trigger the conflict. If you don't see a conflict yet, it may simply not be ready.

Second, open your assigned challenge issue. It tells you which practice file contains the conflict markers.

Third, open that file and search for the start marker. In a browser you can use Control F. In VS Code you can also search directly. Screen reader users can search for the literal characters, since the markers are plain text and fully readable.

Fourth, read both sides carefully.

Fifth, decide: keep one side or combine them.

Sixth, delete all three types of marker lines: the start line, the equals separator, and the end line with the branch name.

Seventh, review the file and search again so there are zero remaining markers.

Eighth, commit your changes on your short-lived feature branch. The recommended naming pattern is fix slash your name dash issue number.

Ninth, open or update your pull request. The suggested title pattern is fix: resolve conflict markers in filename. In the body, include Closes number, with your issue number, and a brief sentence or two explaining what content you kept and why.

[JAMIE]
And when everything is open and passing checks, there's one more administrative step.

[ALEX]
Yes. Post a completion comment on your assigned challenge issue. The example format is: Chapter 7 completed, then the PR number, the filename, and your content decision with a short reason.

[JAMIE]
That matters because this course wants issue-linked evidence, not just a private sense that "I think I fixed it."

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's stay with accessibility for a moment. What should blind or low-vision learners know about navigating this?

[ALEX]
A few key points. The conflict markers themselves are just text, so screen readers can read them directly. Search is your friend. Searching for the start marker is often the fastest way to jump into the conflict area.

If you're on GitHub and can't find the Resolve conflicts button, look on the PR conversation tab near the merge section toward the bottom. Screen reader users may want to search the page for the phrase "Resolve conflicts" button.

For low-vision users, high contrast themes and zoom can make the conflict regions easier to parse, especially in editors that highlight current and incoming changes.

And this chapter also includes learning card guidance for different working styles: visual and mouse users, low vision users, NVDA or JAWS on Windows, VoiceOver on macOS, and CLI users.

[JAMIE]
So the chapter is intentionally not one-size-fits-all.

[ALEX]
Right. Open the guidance that matches how you work.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's talk about spotting a conflict on GitHub. On a pull request, GitHub may show a message that the branch has conflicts that must be resolved before merging.

[JAMIE]
And that's your cue that GitHub needs human help.

[ALEX]
Yes. If the web editor is available, choose Resolve conflicts. GitHub's conflict editor will show the conflicting sections, and your task is to edit the file into one clean final version.

Step by step on GitHub: click Resolve conflicts, edit the file so the markers are removed and the final content is what you want, choose Mark as resolved, and then Commit merge.

[JAMIE]
What does the editor generally feel like?

[ALEX]
It highlights the conflict region and places you right where the disagreement is. But the same rule applies: don't just click through. Read both sides. Decide intentionally.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Now compare that with VS Code.

[ALEX]
In VS Code, conflicts are often shown with highlighted regions and helpful actions above each conflict. Common actions include Accept Current Change, Accept Incoming Change, and Accept Both Changes.

[JAMIE]
And we should translate those a little.

[ALEX]
Yes. "Current" usually means the version currently checked out in your workspace. "Incoming" usually means the version being merged in. "Accept Both" keeps both chunks, after which you may still need to edit for clarity and formatting.

[JAMIE]
So even when the tool gives you buttons, you still need judgment.

[ALEX]
Always. Tooling helps, but it doesn't replace understanding.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
If you cloned the repository and prefer local work, there is a terminal-based alternative.

You update main, switch back to your branch, and merge main into your branch. If a conflict happens, Git pauses the merge and reports the affected files.

Then you open each conflicted file in your editor, look for the markers, remove the markers while keeping the content you want, save the file, mark it resolved with git add, complete the merge with git commit, and push. Your pull request updates automatically.

[JAMIE]
Can we also walk through the command-line conflict reading pattern more explicitly?

[ALEX]
Definitely.

Start the merge that causes the conflict.

Then check which files have conflicts. Look for lines like "both modified" in Git's output.

Open each conflicted file in your editor.

Edit the file: remove the marker lines, keep the content you want.

After editing, mark the file as resolved with git add.

Then complete the merge with git commit. Git often auto-fills the merge commit message.

After that, check the result. Review the diff so you understand what changed. On the PR, review merge state, checks, and overall readiness.

[JAMIE]
That sequence really matters: detect, edit, add, commit, verify.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
There was also a real-file style example in the chapter, where two students both add content to the same table row.

[ALEX]
Yes, and that example is useful because it shows that conflicts aren't always huge. Sometimes two people just edited the same small region, like one row in a Markdown table. The resolution options remain the same: keep one edit, keep the other, or combine them into one clean row that preserves the useful information.

[JAMIE]
So the skill scales from tiny wording changes to larger sections.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Now, something important philosophically: conflicts are not always bad.

[JAMIE]
That sounds surprising.

[ALEX]
A conflict can be evidence that two contributors both cared about the same important area. The conflict forces a deliberate review. In that sense, it can improve quality, because someone must consciously choose the final wording or logic rather than letting one change silently overwrite the other.

[JAMIE]
And the chapter also frames this as relevant to AI-assisted work.

[ALEX]
Yes. Sometimes an AI tool confidently produces changes that overlap with human-written changes. Conflict resolution becomes part of supervising AI safely. You are not just merging text. You are evaluating which content deserves to survive.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Let's cover the most common stuck moments, because learners definitely hit these.

[ALEX]
Absolutely.

If you do not see a conflict, your facilitator may not have triggered it yet. Wait for the signal.

If you cannot find the Resolve conflicts button, check the PR conversation area near the merge section, or search the page for that button label.

If you are not sure what to keep, read both versions aloud. If both are useful, combine them. There is often no single correct answer.

If the autograder still reports conflict markers, search the file for all three marker types. Every one of them must be completely removed.

If you accidentally deleted too much, undo and redo that section carefully.

And if you want a sanity check, ask your facilitator before opening the PR.

[JAMIE]
What about the nuclear option?

[ALEX]
Also valid. If you feel tangled up, you can abandon the attempt and start fresh from a clean copy of the branch or file. Sometimes restarting is faster than untangling confused edits.

[JAMIE]
That's reassuring. Starting over is not cheating.

[ALEX]
Not at all.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
Let's do a compact checklist.

A merge conflict means overlapping edits need a human decision.

Conflict markers are plain text and come in three parts: start marker, separator, end marker.

Read both sides.

Choose one side or combine them.

Delete all marker lines.

Search again to confirm none remain.

Commit the resolution.

Verify the PR status, checks, and diff.

Submit your issue-linked evidence.

[JAMIE]
And emotionally?

[ALEX]
Conflicts are normal. They are manageable. The skill is calm reading and intentional editing.

[PAUSE]

[JAMIE]
Before we wrap up, what are the expected outcomes for this chapter?

[ALEX]
You should be able to identify the three marker lines immediately, read both sides of a conflict, make an intentional content decision, remove all markers, and submit a clean pull request linked to the issue.

[JAMIE]
And that's the learning moment, really. Not "avoid all conflicts forever," but "recognize them without panic and resolve them clearly."

[ALEX]
Exactly. That is the point.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
If you want to check current official guidance beyond the course material, the authoritative sources named for this chapter are GitHub Docs, the GitHub Changelog, GitHub documentation about Git and pull requests, GitHub Flow guidance, and the Git SCM book's discussion of basic merge conflicts.

[JAMIE]
So the course teaches the workflow, and those references are your source of truth when interfaces change.

[ALEX]
Well said.

[PAUSE]

[ALEX]
One final reminder for the challenge: your job is not to preserve the markers. Your job is to produce a clean file that says what the project should actually say.

[JAMIE]
Delete the markers, keep the meaning.

[ALEX]
Perfect. And once you can do that, merge conflicts stop feeling scary.

[JAMIE]
They start feeling like editing.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

# Solution Reference: Challenge 7 -- Resolve a Merge Conflict

This shows what conflict markers look like and how to resolve them.

## What conflict markers look like

When Git cannot automatically merge two changes to the same lines, it inserts markers:

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
Welcome to the Learning Room! This is the main branch version.
=======
Welcome to the Learning Room! This is my improved version with more detail.
>>>>>>> fix/welcome-update
```

### The three sections

- **Between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======`**: The version on the branch you are merging INTO (usually main)
- **Between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`**: The version on YOUR branch
- **The marker lines themselves**: Must be deleted -- they are not content

## Example resolution

**Before (with conflict markers):**

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
Welcome to the Learning Room! This is the main branch version.
=======
Welcome to the Learning Room! This is my improved version with more detail.
>>>>>>> fix/welcome-update
```

**After (resolved):**

```
Welcome to the Learning Room! This is my improved version with more detail.
```

### Decision process

You chose one of three options:

1. **Keep yours:** Delete the HEAD section and all markers, keep your changes
2. **Keep theirs:** Delete your section and all markers, keep the HEAD version
3. **Combine both:** Write new text that incorporates ideas from both versions, delete all markers

All three are valid. The choice depends on which version is better for the project.

## On github.com

GitHub offers a conflict editor directly in the browser:

1. Click "Resolve conflicts" on the PR page
2. The editor highlights conflicting sections
3. Edit the file to remove markers and keep the content you want
4. Click "Mark as resolved" then "Commit merge"

## In VS Code

VS Code highlights conflicts and offers clickable options above each conflict:

- "Accept Current Change" (HEAD version)
- "Accept Incoming Change" (your version)
- "Accept Both Changes" (keeps both, you edit after)

## What matters

The learning objective is understanding that conflicts are normal and resolvable. If you removed all conflict markers and the file makes sense, you completed this challenge.

Use these official references when you need the current source of truth for facts in this chapter.

- [GitHub Docs, home](https://docs.github.com/en)

# Merge Conflicts
>
> **Listen to Episode 7:** [Merge Conflicts Are Not Scary](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix E: Advanced Git](appendix-e-advanced-git.md) | [Appendix G: VS Code Reference](appendix-g-vscode-reference.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: Resolving merge conflicts](https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests/collaborating-with-pull-requests/addressing-merge-conflicts/resolving-a-merge-conflict-on-github) | [Git SCM: Basic Merge Conflicts](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Branching-Basic-Branching-and-Merging#_basic_merge_conflicts)

## Understanding, Preventing, and Resolving Conflicts

> Merge conflicts sound intimidating but are a normal, manageable part of collaborative development. This guide explains what conflicts are, how to read conflict markers, and how to resolve them - step by step.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 7)

Chapter 7 uses **one controlled practice challenge** so students can learn conflict resolution without high-pressure scenarios.

- **Challenge count:** 1
- **Time:** under 10 minutes
- **Evidence:** issue-linked PR and completion comment
- **Pattern:** observe, resolve, verify

### Chapter 7 Challenge Set

1. **Resolve conflict markers** - identify and clean up conflict markers in a practice file, then open a linked PR.

> **Branch guidance for Chapter 7:** Use a short-lived feature branch: `fix/yourname-issueXX` (for example, `fix/maria-issue48`). The same pattern you used in Chapter 6.

### Challenge 7.1 Step-by-Step: Resolve Conflict Markers

**Goal:** Identify the three types of conflict markers in a practice file, decide which content to keep, remove the markers, and submit a clean PR.

> **Agentic strategy:** Sometimes an AI agent will confidently generate code that conflicts with human-written code. Resolving merge conflicts is not just a hurdle for human teamwork; it is exactly how you supervise, correct, and collaborate safely with an AI.

**Where you are working:** your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com (web editor) or in VS Code if you cloned locally.

**Before you start:** Open your **assigned Chapter 7 challenge issue** (the one titled "Chapter 7.1: Resolve Conflict Markers (@yourname)"). The issue description tells you which practice file contains the conflict markers.

Practice sample: [`learning-room/docs/samples/chapter-6-conflict-practice-sample.md`](../learning-room/docs/samples/chapter-6-conflict-practice-sample.md)

1. Open the practice file specified in your challenge issue.
2. Search the file for `<<<<<<<`. This is the **start marker** - it shows where the conflict begins.
3. Read the content between `<<<<<<<` and `=======`. This is **your version** (the current branch).
4. Read the content between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`. This is **their version** (the incoming branch).
5. Decide which content to keep:
   - Keep only your version, or
   - Keep only their version, or
   - Combine both versions into one clean paragraph.
6. Delete all three marker lines:
   - The `<<<<<<< HEAD` line (or similar)
   - The `=======` separator line
   - The `>>>>>>> branch-name` line
7. Review the file to confirm no marker lines remain. Search for `<<<<<<<` again - there should be zero results.
8. Commit your changes on a branch named `fix/yourname-issueXX`.
9. Open a pull request with:
   - Title: `fix: resolve conflict markers in [filename]`
   - Body: Include `Closes #XX` (your challenge issue number) and a 1-2 sentence description of which content you kept and why.

**Screen reader tip:** Use your screen reader's find command (`Ctrl+F` in browser, `Ctrl+H` in VS Code) to jump directly to `<<<<<<<`. The markers are plain text, so they are fully readable.

**You are done when:** Your PR passes bot validation checks and contains no remaining conflict markers.

### Completing Chapter 7: Submit Your Evidence

When your PR is open and passing checks, post a comment on your assigned Chapter 7 challenge issue:

```text
Chapter 7 completed:
- Challenge 7.1: Opened PR #[number] resolving conflict markers in [filename]
- Content decision: kept [your version / their version / combined both] because [reason]
```

### Expected Outcomes

- Student can identify the three conflict marker lines (`<<<<<<<`, `=======`, `>>>>>>>`) immediately.
- Student can read both sides of a conflict and make an intentional content decision.
- Student can remove all markers and submit a clean, issue-linked PR.

### If You Get Stuck

1. Can't find the markers? Use `Ctrl+F` and search for `<<<<<<<` - they are always in sets of three.
2. Not sure which side to keep? Read both versions aloud. Pick the one that is clearer, or combine them.
3. Accidentally deleted too much? Undo with `Ctrl+Z` and start the section over.
4. PR bot says content is wrong? Double-check that zero marker lines remain - search for `<<<<<<<`, `=======`, and `>>>>>>>`.
5. Ask facilitator to sanity-check your final content before opening the PR.
6. Finished but not sure you did it right? Compare your work against the [Challenge 7 reference solution](solutions/solution-07-merge-conflict.md).

### Learning Moment

Merge conflicts are not failures. They are a normal collaboration checkpoint and a chance to make an intentional content decision. In real open source projects, conflicts happen whenever two people edit near the same lines. The skill is not avoiding them - it is resolving them calmly and clearly.

### Learning Pattern Used in This Chapter

1. Start with a controlled, safe conflict (practice file with known markers).
2. Learn to read the conflict structure (your version vs. their version).
3. Make a deliberate content decision (not just deleting randomly).
4. Submit clean evidence through the PR workflow.
5. Build confidence for real conflicts in future contributions.

### About Learning Cards in This Chapter

This chapter provides learning cards: expandable blocks that offer perspective-specific guidance for different ways of working. Not every card appears at every step. Open the ones that match how you work.

The following table describes the five learning card types used in this chapter.

## What Is a Merge Conflict?

A merge conflict occurs when two people have both changed the **same part of the same file** in **different ways**, and Git cannot automatically decide which version is correct.

Git can merge changes automatically when they touch different parts of a file. Conflicts only happen when two changes overlap - for example:

- Person A changed line 12 to say "Submit form"
- Person B changed line 12 to say "Send message"
- Git asks: which one do you want to keep?

## Why Conflicts Happen

The most common causes:

| Cause | Example |
| -------  | ---------  |
| Two people edited the same line | You both fixed the same typo differently |
| One person deleted a file but another edited it | You removed an old function; they fixed a bug in it |
| Two people restructured the same section | You reorganized a list; they added items to it |
| A long-running PR diverged from main | Your branch is weeks old and main has changed significantly |

## How to Prevent Conflicts (Prevention is Easier Than Resolution)

Avoiding conflicts in the first place saves time and reduces stress. Here are the most effective strategies:

### 1. **Keep your branches short-lived**

Work in small, focused chunks. A branch that lives for 3 days has far fewer conflicts than one that lives for 3 weeks.

- Target: 1-3 days from branch to merge
- If a feature takes longer, break it into smaller PRs

### 2. **Sync with main frequently**

The longer your branch diverges from main, the more likely conflicts become.

**Best practice:** Sync daily if main is active:

```bash
# From your feature branch
git fetch origin
git merge origin/main
# Or: git rebase origin/main (if comfortable with rebasing)
```

**GitHub web method:** Use the "Update branch" button on your PR if it appears.

### 3. **Communicate with your team**

Let others know what files you're working on. Use issue comments:

> "Heads up: I'm working on the `[TODO]` sections in `docs/welcome.md` for Challenge 3. If you're also editing welcome.md, let's coordinate so we don't conflict."

In the Learning Room, this is especially important because multiple students may claim challenges that touch the same file. Challenges 1 and 3 both modify `docs/welcome.md` - if two students work on both simultaneously without coordinating, a merge conflict will occur.

### 4. **Avoid mass reformatting**

Running a formatter on an entire file creates conflicts with anyone else editing that file. If you must:

- Do it in a **separate PR** before functional changes
- Announce it to the team
- Merge it quickly so everyone can sync

### 5. **Pull before you push**

Always fetch and merge (or pull) before pushing your changes:

```bash
git pull origin main  # Sync your local main
git checkout your-branch
git merge main        # Merge main into your branch
git push              # Now push
```

This catches conflicts locally where they're easier to resolve.

### 6. **Work on separate files when possible**

If multiple people are working simultaneously, divide tasks by files or modules rather than everyone touching the same code.

### 7. **Keep PRs small**

A 50-file PR will almost certainly conflict with something. A 5-file PR merges quickly and cleanly.

The most effective contributors make many small PRs rather than one giant one.

### 8. **Use Draft PRs for early visibility**

Open your PR as a draft while still working. Others can see what you're changing and avoid overlapping work. Convert to "Ready for review" when done.

## Advanced Prevention: Understanding Fast-Forward Merges

When your branch is perfectly up to date with main and adds new commits on top, GitHub can do a "fast-forward" merge - main simply moves forward to your latest commit. No merge commit needed. No possibility of conflicts.

**How to achieve this:** Rebase your branch on main right before merging:

```bash
git checkout your-branch
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main
git push --force-with-lease  # See warning below about force pushing
```

**Warning:** Force pushing rewrites history. Only do this on branches you alone control (not shared branches). Never force push to `main`.

For more on force pushing and rebasing, see the [Glossary](appendix-a-glossary.md#force-push).

## When Conflicts Are Actually Good

Conflicts indicate that multiple people are actively improving the project. In a healthy, collaborative environment, occasional conflicts are normal and manageable.

If you never have conflicts, it might mean:

- You're the only contributor (less review, less learning)
- PRs are moving too slowly (stagnation)
- People are avoiding working on important files (technical debt)

**The goal isn't zero conflicts.** The goal is catching them early, resolving them cleanly, and learning patterns that reduce future conflicts.

## Conflict Markers - What They Mean

When conflict markers appear in a file, your editor is showing you both versions of the conflicted content so you can choose. The format is always:

```text
<<<<<<< HEAD
The content that is on YOUR current branch
=======
The content coming from the OTHER branch (or main)
>>>>>>> branch-name-or-commit-hash
```

### Breakdown

- `<<<<<<< HEAD` - the start of YOUR version (HEAD = "the branch you are currently on")
- `=======` - the dividing line between the two versions
- `>>>>>>> branch-name` - the end of the INCOMING version (from the branch being merged in)

### Example in a real file

#### Original file (`docs/keyboard-shortcuts.md`) before conflict

```markdown
| Insert+Space | Toggle between Browse Mode and Focus Mode |
```

#### After two students both added a shortcut to the same table row

```
<<<<<<< HEAD
  Insert+Space -- Toggle between Browse Mode and Focus Mode
  Insert+F5 -- List elements by type
=======
  Insert+Space -- Toggle between Browse Mode and Focus Mode
  Insert+F7 -- Elements list (links, headings, form fields)
>>>>>>> add-nvda-shortcut
```

#### Resolution options

1. Keep your version: add only `Insert+F5`
2. Keep their version: add only `Insert+F7`
3. Keep both rows: add both shortcuts to the table (often the right answer when two students added different valid shortcuts)

## When You Feel Stuck

### Ask for help - it's normal

If you are unsure which version to keep:

1. Leave a comment on the PR: "I have a merge conflict in `filename.js` and I'm not sure which version to keep - could someone help me understand the intent of these two changes?"
2. Tag the PR author or a maintainer with `@username`

### Abandon and start fresh (nuclear option)

If a conflict is severe (the branch diverged a lot from main):

1. Close the PR without merging
2. Start a new branch from the latest `main`
3. Apply only your intended changes to the new branch
4. Open a new PR

This is legitimate - not a failure.

> - **In the cloud** - GitHub Agentic Workflows can detect stale PRs diverging from `main` and automatically notify contributors with a suggested rebase checklist - preventing the conflict before it is ever introduced
>
> *Understanding conflict markers is not a stepping stone to letting AI handle conflicts. It is the skill that tells you when AI got it wrong.*

# Assignment 1: You Belong Here

Welcome to Git Going with GitHub! This is your private learning repository for Day 1. Everything you do here is yours -- experiment freely.

## What You Will Do Today

During the live Day 1 core path, you will practice the skills needed to make your first browser-based GitHub contribution. If the room needs more time, later challenges can continue during open lab time or after the event.

- Navigate a real GitHub repository using your screen reader
- File your first issue describing something you noticed
- Communicate with teammates using @mentions and comments
- Create a branch to work in safely
- Make your first commit to a file
- Open a pull request linking your work to an issue
- Learn how merge conflicts work, with live support if time allows
- Reflect on open source culture and communication, live or asynchronously
- Merge a pull request into the main branch, or leave with clear next steps to finish it

## Challenges

Complete these challenges in order. Each one builds on the previous. When you close a challenge issue, the Student Progression Bot automatically opens your next challenge. The live agenda prioritizes Challenges 1-6; Challenges 7-9 are available as stretch or async follow-up.

| Challenge | What You Do | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Find Your Way Around | Explore the repository structure and locate key files | [Chapter 3](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/03-navigating-repositories.md) |
| 2. File Your First Issue | Create an issue describing something you noticed | [Chapter 5](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/05-working-with-issues.md) |
| 3. Join the Conversation | Mention a teammate or bot using @mentions | [Chapter 5](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/05-working-with-issues.md) |
| 4. Branch Out | Create a feature branch for your work | [Chapter 4](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/04-the-learning-room.md) |
| 5. Make Your Mark | Edit a file and commit with a clear message | [Chapter 4](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/04-the-learning-room.md) |
| 6. Open Your First Pull Request | Open a PR that references an issue with `Closes #N` | [Chapter 6](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/06-working-with-pull-requests.md) |
| 7. Survive a Merge Conflict | Understand and fix conflict markers | [Chapter 7](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/07-merge-conflicts.md) |
| 8. The Culture Layer | Reflect on community norms and communication | [Chapter 8](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/08-open-source-culture.md) |
| 9. Merge Day | Get your PR reviewed, approved, and merged | [Chapter 10](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/10-notifications-and-day-1-close.md) |

## Automated Checks

Challenges 2, 5, 6, and 7 have automated checks that run as GitHub Actions inside your repo:

- **Challenge 2:** Verifies you have filed at least one issue
- **Challenge 5:** Verifies at least one commit exists on a non-default branch
- **Challenge 6:** Verifies your PR body contains `Closes`, `Fixes`, or `Resolves`
- **Challenge 7:** Verifies no merge conflict markers remain in `docs/`

Each check posts a single comment on the relevant issue or pull request and updates it whenever you push a new change. If a check fails, read the comment and push an update.

## Evidence

Each challenge has an issue that the Student Progression Bot creates for you. Complete the challenge, leave a comment with your evidence, and close the issue to unlock the next one.

## If You Get Stuck

Every chapter has an "If You Get Stuck" section with specific troubleshooting steps. Start there.

You can also:

- Ask your assigned buddy or study group
- Post a question on the issue thread
- Mention `@gandalf-bot` in a comment for a workspace check
- Ask a facilitator for help -- that is what they are here for

## After Day 1

When you complete all 9 challenges, you have the foundation for everything in Day 2 -- or for contributing to any open source project on your own. These skills are yours permanently.

**Continuing to Day 2?** See the [Day 2 assignment](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/classroom/assignment-day2-you-can-build-this.md) for what comes next.

**Day 1 is your only day?** Everything you learned today is complete and self-contained. See the [Next Steps guide](https://github.com/Community-Access/git-going-with-github/blob/main/docs/21-next-steps.md) for how to continue your GitHub journey independently.
